choices: The strategy that gives the highest number in the matrix
The strategy the opponent is currently playing
A strategy that gives the highest payoff regardless of the opponent's action
A strategy that guarantees the best worst case
explain: Best against EVERY opposing choice. The best worst case is the secure (maximin) strategy.

stem: True or false: Every player in every game has a dominant strategy.
explain: False. Dillard's has none in the in-class exercise.

stem: If you have no dominant strategy but your rival does, the textbook says you should:
choices: Assume the rival plays its dominant strategy and choose your best response to it
explain: Put yourself in your rival's shoes.

choices: Guarantees the highest payoff in the worst case
Is always the same as a dominant strategy
explain: It is cautious and can ignore what a rational rival will actually do.

choices: It is never part of an equilibrium in any game
It gives a negative payoff somewhere
Another strategy gives a higher payoff against every opposing choice
explain: A rational player never plays a strictly dominated strategy, so it can be crossed out.

stem:
Firm X (rows) and Firm Y (columns):

| X \ Y | Left | Right |
|---|---|---|
| Top | 8, 3 | 12, 9 |
| Bottom | 5, 6 | 4, 2 |

Who has a dominant strategy?
explain: X's best responses: vs Left: Top; vs Right: Top. Y's best responses: vs Top: Right; vs Bottom: Left. A player whose best response never changes has a dominant strategy.

stem:
Player A (rows) and Player B (columns):

| A \ B | Left | Right |
|---|---|---|
| Up | 10, 20 | 15, 8 |
| Down | -10, 7 | 10, 10 |

Who has a dominant strategy?
explain: A's best responses: vs Left: Up; vs Right: Up. B's best responses: vs Up: Left; vs Down: Right. A player whose best response never changes has a dominant strategy.

stem:
Dillard's (rows) and Nordstrom (columns):

| Dillard's \ Nordstrom | Girl's | Women's |
|---|---|---|
| Girl's | 2, 1 | 4, 2 |
| Women's | 6, 4 | 3, 5 |

Who has a dominant strategy?
explain: Dillard's's best responses: vs Girl's: Women's; vs Women's: Girl's. Nordstrom's best responses: vs Girl's: Women's; vs Women's: Women's. A player whose best response never changes has a dominant strategy.

stem:
Using the Visa matrix:

| Visa \ Mastercard | Lower Fee | Maintain Fee |
|---|---|---|
| Lower Fee | 2, 2 | 4, 1 |
| Maintain Fee | 1, 4 | 3, 3 |

Why is Lower Fee dominant for Visa?
choices: It pays more whether Mastercard lowers (2 > 1) or maintains (4 > 3)
It gives Visa the highest number in the table
explain: Slide p. 22: no matter what Mastercard does, Visa's best option is to lower.

stem:
Nordstrom's dominant strategy is to feature Women's. What should Dillard's do?

| Dillard's \ Nordstrom | Girl's | Women's |
|---|---|---|
| Girl's | 2, 1 | 4, 2 |
| Women's | 6, 4 | 3, 5 |
choices: Feature Girl's, its best response to Women's (4 > 3)
Feature Women's, since 6 is the biggest payoff
explain: Expect the rival to play its dominant strategy and best-respond. 6 is only available if Nordstrom picks Girl's, which it will not.

stem:
In the 3 by 3 game below, which column strategy is strictly dominated?

| Row \ Column | Left | Center | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | 4, 3 | 5, 1 | 6, 2 |
| Middle | 2, 1 | 8, 4 | 3, 6 |
| Bottom | 3, 0 | 9, 6 | 2, 8 |
choices: Center (Right beats it in every row)
explain: Column payoffs: Center 1, 4, 6 versus Right 2, 6, 8. Right is higher in every row.

stem:
Game Theory Exercise Part 1:

| Facebook \ Twitter | Ban | Don't Ban |
|---|---|---|
| Ban | -350, -3 | -350, 23 |
| Don't Ban | -277, -3 | -280, -12 |

Who has a dominant strategy?
explain: Facebook: -277 > -350 and -280 > -350. Twitter: 23 > -3 if Facebook bans, but -3 > -12 if it doesn't, so no dominant strategy.

stem: True or false: In Game Theory Exercise Part 3, Facebook still has a dominant strategy.
explain: False. It bans if Twitter doesn't (-350 > -420) and doesn't ban if Twitter bans (-137 > -350).
